label: thm:main-counterexample
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-counterexample}
The ring $R$ in \eqref{eq:main-ring} is commutative, coherent,
local, nonnoetherian, and of Krull dimension zero.
There is a countably generated PGF $R$-module $B$ such that, for the injective
$R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $I=D(R)$, one has
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,B^{\mathbb N})\ne0$ for every $n\ge1$.
Consequently, $\operatorname{Gfd}_R B^{\mathbb N}=\infty$.
There are a countably generated free $R$-module $Q$ and an
endomorphism $\delta:Q\to Q$ such that
$B=\ker\delta=\operatorname{im}\delta$, $\delta^2=0$, and the periodic complex
$(Q,\delta)$, with $Q$ in every degree and differential $\delta$,
remains exact after tensoring with every injective $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module.
head: environment

label: thm:main-duality
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{thm:main-duality}
Let $R$ be the ring and $B$ the module in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample}. Put
$E=B^+$. Then $E$ is pure-injective and Ding injective, but
$\operatorname{Gfd}_R E^+=\infty$ and $\operatorname{Gid}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}E^{++}=\infty$.
head: environment

label: thm:criteria
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:criteria}
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. Fix $T$, its free presentation,
and $\mathcal S$ as above. The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The class $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under arbitrary direct products.
\item Every direct product of at most $\rho$ Gorenstein flat modules has
finite Gorenstein flat dimension.
\item The module $L$ is $\mathcal{GF}(R)$-Mittag--Leffler.
\item The module $L$ is $E_U$-stationary.
\item The module $C_U^{++}$ is Gorenstein flat.
\item The module $E_U^{++}$ has finite Gorenstein injective dimension.
\item The class $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is definable.
\item Every $R$-module has a Gorenstein flat preenvelope.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem:character-Tor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:character-Tor}\label{lem:product-into-bidual}
Let $T$ be an $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module, $M$ an $R$-module, and $q\ge0$.
Then there are natural isomorphisms
$\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,M)^+\cong\operatorname{Ext}^q_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(T,M^+)
\cong\operatorname{Ext}_R^q(M,T^+)$.
A pure monomorphism $N\to M$ induces a monomorphism
$\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,N)\to\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,M)$.
For $q\ge1$, the class
$\mathcal A_q(T)=\{M:\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,M)=0\}$ is closed under pure
submodules, pure quotients, direct summands, and direct limits.
For every family $(M_i)$ of $R$-modules, there is a pure
monomorphism $\prod_iM_i\to(\bigoplus_iM_i)^{++}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The isomorphisms follow from \cite[p.~241]{Lambek}, applied to $R$ and $R^{\mathrm{op}}$.
If $0\to N\to M\to D\to0$ is pure, its character dual splits
(see \cite[Proposition 9.1]{Stenstrom}). Thus the dual of
$\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,N)\to\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(T,M)$ is a split epimorphism,
so this Tor map is a monomorphism. The splitting also gives
$M^+\cong D^+\oplus N^+$, so the Tor--Ext isomorphism gives
closure under pure submodules and pure quotients.
Closure under direct summands follows from additivity of Tor.
Closure under direct limits follows because Tor commutes with
direct limits. For the pure embedding, see the proof of
$(ii)\Rightarrow(iv)$ in \cite[Theorem 4.4]{MP}.
head: environment

label: lem:explicit-ring
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:explicit-ring}
The ring properties asserted in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample} hold for $R$.
It is free over every $R_N$ for $N\ge0$ and over every
$A_0\otimes A_j$ for $j\ge1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The monomials obtained by choosing at most one of $x_j,y_j$ for
each $j$, with only finitely many indices used, form a $k$-basis
of $R$. Those using only indices greater than $N$ form an
$R_N$-basis of $R$. For $j\ge1$, those using neither index $0$
nor index $j$ form an $A_0\otimes A_j$-basis.
The monomial $k$-basis of $R$ is countably infinite, so $|R|=|k|+\aleph_0$.
Every finite matrix over $R$ has its entries in some $R_N$.
Since $R_N$ is finite-dimensional, the kernel of this matrix over $R_N$ is
finitely generated. Flat base change identifies the kernel over $R$
with the scalar extension of that kernel. Therefore every finite matrix over $R$ has finitely
generated kernel, and $R$ is coherent (see \cite{Chase,GT}).

Let $\mathfrak m$ be the augmentation ideal of $R$.
Every element of $\mathfrak m$ is nilpotent in some $R_N$, whereas
an element with nonzero constant coefficient is a unit in a
subring $R_N$ containing it. Hence $\mathfrak m$ is the unique maximal ideal and
the nilradical. It follows that $R$ has Krull dimension zero.
The classes of $x_j,y_j$ are linearly independent in
$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. Thus $\mathfrak m$ is not finitely
generated, and $R$ is not noetherian.
head: environment

label: lem:finite-complete
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define a $k$-linear map $h:F_0\to F_0$ by
$h(e_n)=0$, $h(x_0e_n)=e_{2n}$, and
$h(y_0e_n)=e_{2n+1}$.
Then $dh+hd=1$, and $h\otimes1$ commutes with $1\otimes t_j$.
Consequently,
$$
 \Delta_j\begin{pmatrix}h\otimes1&0\\0&-h\otimes1\end{pmatrix}
 +\begin{pmatrix}h\otimes1&0\\0&-h\otimes1\end{pmatrix}\Delta_j=1.
$$
Thus $(U_j,\Delta_j)$ is exact.

Let $\epsilon_j,a_{x_j},a_{y_j}$ be the basis of $D(A_j)$
dual to $1,x_j,y_j$.
The differential on $D(A_j)\otimes_{A_j}V_j$ sends
$a_{x_j}f_n$ to $\epsilon_jf_{2n}$,
$a_{y_j}f_n$ to $\epsilon_jf_{2n+1}$, and
$\epsilon_jf_n$ to zero.
It has a $k$-linear contraction $h'$ defined by
$h'(\epsilon_jf_{2n})=a_{x_j}f_n$,
$h'(\epsilon_jf_{2n+1})=a_{y_j}f_n$, and
$h'(a_{x_j}f_n)=h'(a_{y_j}f_n)=0$.
Since $\Lambda_j$ is finite-dimensional, one has
$$
 D(\Lambda_j)\otimes_{\Lambda_j}U_j
 \cong\bigl((D(A_0)\otimes_{A_0}F_0)
       \otimes(D(A_j)\otimes_{A_j}V_j)\bigr)^{\oplus2}.
$$
Under this identification, the differential $1\otimes\Delta_j$
has the same block matrix, with the maps induced by $d$ and $t_j$.
The map $1\otimes h'$ contracts the differential induced by $t_j$
and commutes with the differential induced by $d$.
Hence
$$
 (1\otimes\Delta_j)
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\otimes h'\\1\otimes h'&0\end{pmatrix}
 +\begin{pmatrix}0&1\otimes h'\\1\otimes h'&0\end{pmatrix}
 (1\otimes\Delta_j)=1.
$$
This proves exactness after tensoring with $D(\Lambda_j)$.

Finally, every injective $\Lambda_j^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $J$ is a direct
summand of a direct sum of copies of $D(\Lambda_j)$.
Indeed, $a\mapsto[b\mapsto ab]$ embeds $J$ into
$\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Lambda_j,J)\congD(\Lambda_j)\otimes J$.
The embedding splits by injectivity. A vector-space basis of $J$
expresses the latter module as a direct sum of copies of
$D(\Lambda_j)$. Tensor products preserve direct sums and summands.
Thus $(U_j,\Delta_j)$ remains exact after tensoring with every injective $J$.
Note that the contractions need only be $k$-linear.
head: environment

label: eq:restricted-detection
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove that $\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,\prod_jB_j)\ne0$ for every $n\ge1$.
Let $a_y,\epsilon_0\inD(A_0)$ extract the $y_0$-coefficient
and the constant coefficient, respectively.
Then $a_yx_0=0$. For every $f\inD(A_0)$,
$f x_0=f(x_0)\epsilon_0$ and
$f y_0=f(y_0)\epsilon_0$.
Define $\eta=a_y\otimes e_0$ in
$D(A_0)\otimes_{A_0}F_0$ and define the linear functional
$\lambda(\sum_na_n\otimes e_n)=a_0(y_0)$.
Then $\eta$ is a cycle, $\lambda(\eta)=1$, and
$\lambda(1\otimes d)=0$.

Put $w_j=x_jf_0\in V_j$.
For $b=\sum_n b_nf_n$, let
$\mu_j(b)=[x_j]b_0-[y_j]b_1$, where $[x_j]$ and $[y_j]$ mean
coefficient extraction in the basis $1,x_j,y_j$.
Note that $t_jw_j=0$ and $\mu_j(w_j)=1$.
In $t_j(b)$, the two extracted coefficients are both the constant
coefficient of $b_0$. Thus $\mu_jt_j=0$.
Since $\lambda$ and $\mu_j$ vanish on the images of the
differentials induced by $d$ and $t_j$, respectively,
the cycle $u_j=(\eta\otimes w_j,0)$ in
$D(A_0)\otimes_{A_0}U_j$ and the functional
$\ell_j=(\lambda\otimes\mu_j,0)$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:restricted-detection}
 \ell_j(u_j)=1,\qquad \ell_j(1\otimes\Delta_j)=0.
\end{equation}
Hence $u_j$ is not a boundary.

The $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $I=D(R)$ is injective, since
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(M,D(R))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,k)$ for $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-modules $M$.
The right action is $(f r)(a)=f(ra)$.
Define $i\in I$ by
$i(a\otimes s)=a_y(a)\epsilon(s)$ for $a\in A_0$ and
$s\in\bigotimes_{j\ge1}A_j$, where $\epsilon$ is the augmentation
of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}A_j$.
Put $q_j=(e_0\otimes w_j,0)\in Q_j$,
$W=\prod_{j\ge1}Q_j$, and $\partial=\prod_j\delta_j$.
Then
$$
 z=i\otimes(q_j)_j\in I\otimes_RW.
$$
Since $\delta_jq_j=x_0q_j$ and $ix_0=0$, $z$ is a cycle.
The same formula gives a cycle $z_N$ in $I\otimes_{R_N}W$ for
every $N$.

Fix $N$ and choose $j>N$.
Put $C_N=\bigotimes_{1\le r\le N}A_r$ and
$S_{N,j}=\bigotimes_{r>N,\ r\ne j}A_r$.
Then $R=A_0\otimes C_N\otimes A_j\otimes S_{N,j}$ and
$Q_j=U_j\otimes C_N\otimes S_{N,j}$ after reordering factors.
For $f\in I$ and $c\in C_N$, let
$f_c(a)=f(a\otimes c\otimes1\otimes1)$ for $a\in A_0$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-restriction}
 \begin{aligned}
 r_{N,j}:I\otimes_{R_N}Q_j&\longrightarrow
                         D(A_0)\otimes_{A_0}U_j,\\
 f\otimes(q\otimes c\otimes s)&\longmapsto
                         \epsilon(s)(f_c\otimes_{A_0}q).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Balancing over $C_N$ multiplies $c$ in the same way on both sides.
Balancing over $A_0$ uses $f_c a\otimes q=f_c\otimes aq$.
Thus the map is well defined.
The map $r_{N,j}$ acts componentwise on the two summands and
commutes with every block of the differential, since each block
acts only on $U_j$. Note that $r_{N,j}$ is defined for every
$f\inD(R)$.

Let $p_j:W\to Q_j$ be the coordinate projection.
The composite $\ell_jr_{N,j}(1\otimes p_j)$ kills every boundary
and takes value one on $z_N$, by \eqref{eq:restricted-detection}.
Hence $z_N$ is not a boundary for any $N$.

It follows that $z$ is not a boundary over $R$.
Indeed, let $V_0=I\otimes_kW$, and let $H_N$ be the span of
$(fr)\otimes w-f\otimes rw$ with $f\in I$, $w\in W$, and $r\in R_N$.
Then $I\otimes_{R_N}W=V_0/H_N$.
The subspace generated by all $R$-balancing relations is
$\bigcup_NH_N$, since each finite linear combination involves
only finitely many scalars from $R$.
If $z=(1\otimes\partial)b$ over $R$, representatives of the two
sides in $V_0$ would differ by an element of some $H_N$.
Then $z_N$ would be a boundary, a contradiction.
The argument applies to arbitrary elements of $I$ and $W$,
including tuples in $W$ with infinitely many nonzero coordinates.

To compute the Tor groups, put $P=\prod_jB_j$ and take
direct products of the exact sequences
$0\to B_j\to Q_j\to B_j\to0$. This gives
$0\to P\to W\xrightarrow{\overline\partial}P\to0$.
Since $R$ is coherent, $W$ is flat by \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Chase}.
Thus the repeated maps $\partial$ give a flat resolution
$$
 \cdots\xrightarrow{\partial}W\xrightarrow{\partial}W
       \xrightarrow{\overline\partial}P\longrightarrow0.
$$
The cycle $z$, which is not a boundary, shows that
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,P)=H(I\otimes_RW,1\otimes\partial)\ne0$ for all $n\ge1$.
Hence $\operatorname{Gfd}_RP=\infty$ by the Tor vanishing recalled in
Subsection~\ref{sec:gorenstein-modules}.

It remains to construct $B$ and obtain the assertions for its
countable power. The ring properties follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:explicit-ring}.
Put $Q=\bigoplus_jQ_j$, $\delta=\bigoplus_j\delta_j$, and
$B=\bigoplus_jB_j$. Then $Q$ is countably generated and free,
$\ker\delta=\operatorname{im}\delta=B$, and the periodic complex remains exact
after tensoring with every injective $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module. Thus $B$ is PGF and countably generated.
The coordinatewise inclusions $B_j\to B$ and projections $B\to B_j$
split $P=\prod_jB_j$ off $B^{\mathbb N}$.
They induce split maps on Tor. Therefore
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,B^{\mathbb N})\ne0$ for all $n\ge1$.
The same Tor vanishing gives the dimension assertion.
head: environment

label: rmk:tensor-comparison
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:tensor-comparison}
Note that $q_j=x_j(E_{0,0},0)$ and $ix_j=0$.
Thus every coordinate image of $z$ is zero, but $z$ is a nonzero
cycle which is not a boundary. In particular, the comparison map
$I\otimes_R\prod_jQ_j\to\prod_j(I\otimes_RQ_j)$ is not injective.
Each coordinate vanishing uses the scalar $x_j$.
An equality in a tensor product follows from finitely many
of its defining relations, whereas $z_N$ is not a boundary over
any $R_N$, as proved after \eqref{eq:finite-restriction}.
Thus coherence does not ensure that the complex
$(W,\partial)$ remains exact after tensoring with injective modules.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-rings-union
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-rings-union}
Each ring $R_N$ in Subsection~\ref{sec:periodic-complex} has Gorenstein flat
modules closed under arbitrary direct products. The inclusions
$R_N\to R_{N+1}$ make $R_{N+1}$ a free $R_N$-module, whereas Gorenstein flat
$R$-modules are not closed under direct products.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each $R_N$ is a commutative artinian local ring, hence complete,
and admits a dualizing complex; see the proof of
\cite[Theorem 5.10]{CFH}.
Therefore Gorenstein flat $R_N$-modules are closed under direct
products by \cite[Theorem 5.7]{CFH}.
The basis of $A_{N+1}$ shows that $R_{N+1}$ is free over $R_N$.
Failure over the union follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample}.
head: environment

label: rmk:nonmaximal-localizations
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:nonmaximal-localizations}
Let $R$ be the ring in \eqref{eq:main-ring}, and let $\mathfrak m$
be its augmentation ideal. Then $\operatorname{Spec}R=\{\mathfrak m\}$,
so $R$ has no nonmaximal prime ideals. In
\cite[Proposition 6.21]{MS}, Murfet and Salarian assume that the
localization at every nonmaximal prime ideal is Gorenstein.
This localization hypothesis is vacuous for $R$.
Since $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is not closed under direct products by
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample}, the noetherian hypothesis in
\cite[Proposition 6.21]{MS} cannot be replaced by coherence.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $P=\prod_jB_j$. There is
a pure monomorphism $P\to B^{++}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:product-into-bidual}. Pure monomorphisms induce
monomorphisms on $\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,-)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:character-Tor}. The nonvanishing of $\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,P)$
established in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample}
therefore gives $\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(I,B^{++})\ne0$ for every $n\ge1$.
The Tor vanishing recalled in Subsection~\ref{sec:gorenstein-modules}
gives $\operatorname{Gfd}_RB^{++}=\infty$.
Since $E^+=B^{++}$, this also proves $\operatorname{Gfd}_RE^+=\infty$.

Character modules are pure-injective, so $E=B^+$ is pure-injective.
Since $B$ is Gorenstein flat, $E$ is Ding injective by
\cite[Lemma 2.8]{MD}.
Finally,
$\operatorname{Gid}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}E^{++}=\operatorname{Gfd}_RB^{++}=\infty$ by
\cite[Proposition 3.11]{Holm}.
head: environment

label: cor:duality-failures
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Definable classes are closed under character biduals
(see \cite[Corollary 4.6]{MP}).
Thus the assertions about $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ and $\mathcal{GI}(R^{\mathrm{op}})$
follow from Corollary~\ref{thm:main-duality}.
Since $R$ is nonnoetherian, the Ding injective $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-modules
are not closed under direct sums by \cite[Proposition 2.7]{MD}
and hence do not form a definable class.

Take $E=B^+$. Since ${}_RR$ is free, $R^+$ is an injective $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module. Tensor--Hom adjunction gives
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(E,R^+)\cong E^+$, so
$\operatorname{Gfd}_R\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(E,R^+)=\infty$ by
Corollary~\ref{thm:main-duality}.

For the final assertion, suppose that $e:M\longrightarrow G$ is a
Gorenstein flat preenvelope. Each projection
$p_j:M\longrightarrow B$ factors as $h_je$.
The map $h=(h_j):G\longrightarrow M$ then satisfies $he=1_M$.
Hence $M$ is a direct summand of a Gorenstein flat module, so it is
Gorenstein flat by \cite[Theorem 3.7]{Holm}, a contradiction.
The same proof applies to a projectively coresolved Gorenstein flat
preenvelope, since $B$ belongs to that class and that class is contained
in $\mathcal{GF}(R)$.
head: environment

label: rmk:character-duality
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:character-duality}\label{rmk:noetherian-hypothesis}
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. For an $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $J$,
applying the character-duality equivalence recalled in
Subsection~\ref{sec:character-modules} to $M=J^+$ shows that
$J^+$ is Gorenstein flat if and only if $J^{++}$ is Ding injective.
 For the ring in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample},
there is a Ding injective module
$E=B^+$ with $\operatorname{Gfd}_RE^+=\infty$ by Corollary~\ref{thm:main-duality}.

Since Ding injective modules are Gorenstein injective,
there are a Gorenstein injective
module $E$ and an injective module $I$ over the commutative
coherent ring in \eqref{eq:main-ring} with
$\operatorname{Gfd}_R\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(E,I)=\infty$ by
Corollary~\ref{cor:Hom-injective}.
Consequently, the question of Christensen, Foxby and Holm
(see \cite[Question 4.26]{Survey}) has a negative answer when its
noetherian hypothesis is replaced by coherence.
head: environment

label: lem:detecting-dimensions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:detecting-dimensions}
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. Choose $T$ as in
\eqref{eq:detecting-test}. For every $d\ge0$, an $R$-module $M$ and
an $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $J$ satisfy
$$
 \operatorname{Gfd}_RM\le d\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \operatorname{Tor}_{d+1}^R(T,M)=0,
 \quad
 \operatorname{Gid}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}J\le d\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \operatorname{Ext}^{d+1}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(T,J)=0.
$$
Moreover, $\operatorname{Gfd}_RM=\operatorname{Gid}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}M^+$.
For each $d\ge0$, the class of $R$-modules of Gorenstein flat
dimension at most $d$ is closed under pure submodules and direct
summands.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L_d$ be the $d$th syzygy in a free resolution of $M$, with
$L_0=M$. Dimension shifting gives
$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(T,L_d)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{d+1}^R(T,M)$.
Thus vanishing implies $L_d\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$ and $\operatorname{Gfd}_RM\le d$.
Since $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is resolving, every syzygy of a Gorenstein flat
module is Gorenstein flat. Hence all positive Tor groups with $T$
vanish on $\mathcal{GF}(R)$. A finite Gorenstein flat resolution and its
long exact Tor sequences give the converse.

For the $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $J$, use the $d$th cosyzygy of an injective
coresolution of $J$. The condition that this cosyzygy belongs to
$\mathcal{GI}(R^{\mathrm{op}})$ is $\operatorname{Ext}^{d+1}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(T,J)=0$. Conversely, heredity of the
cotorsion pair gives vanishing of all positive Ext groups from $T$
on $\mathcal{GI}(R^{\mathrm{op}})$. A finite Gorenstein injective coresolution gives the
required vanishing. The equality $\operatorname{Gfd}_RM=\operatorname{Gid}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}M^+$ follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:character-Tor} and also from
\cite[Proposition 3.11]{Holm}. The final assertion follows by
applying Lemma~\ref{lem:character-Tor} in degree $d+1$.
head: environment

label: thm:coordinate
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:coordinate}
Let $T$ be an $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-module and $n\ge1$. If $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ is a
family of $R$-modules and
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(T,\prod_{i\in I}M_i)\ne0$, then there is
$X\subseteq I$ with $|X|\le\rho$ such that
$\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(T,\prod_{i\in X}M_i)\ne0$.
Consequently, $\mathcal A_n(T)$ is closed under arbitrary direct products
if and only if it is closed under direct products with at most $\rho$
factors.

Let $R$ be a right coherent ring, and let $(G_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in
$\mathcal{GF}(R)$. Then $\prod_{i\in I}G_i$ is Gorenstein flat if and only
if every direct product over a subset of the index set with at most
$\rho$ factors is Gorenstein flat. In particular, if $R$ is countable, $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under
countable direct products if and only if it is closed under arbitrary direct products.
head: environment

label: eq:boundary-matrix
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a free resolution $F_\bullet$ of $T$ and bases of its terms.
Set $P=\prod_iM_i$. Choose a cycle representing a nonzero class,
and write it as $z=\sum_{j=1}^m e_j\otimes a_j$, where the $e_j$
are distinct basis vectors of $F_n$ and $a_j\in P$.

For each finite subset of the basis of $F_{n+1}$, write the images
of its elements using $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ and the additional basis
vectors which occur. A preimage of $z$ involving only the basis
vectors in this subset exists
exactly when a finite system of the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundary-matrix}
 \varphi(\mathbf a):\quad
 \exists\mathbf y\ (A\mathbf y=\mathbf a\ \text{and}\ B\mathbf y=0)
\end{equation}
has a solution, where $A$ and $B$ are finite matrices over $R$
and $\mathbf a$ is the column vector with entries $a_1,\ldots,a_m$.
The second block imposes zero coefficients on all
additional basis vectors. Every preimage of $z$ in
$F_{n+1}\otimes_RP$ involves only finitely many basis vectors of
$F_{n+1}$, so these systems characterize the boundaries whose
coefficients vanish outside $e_1,\ldots,e_m$.

Only the sizes and entries of $A$ and $B$ occur in
\eqref{eq:boundary-matrix}; the names of additional basis vectors
do not occur. There are at most $\rho$ distinct such systems.
Denote their set by $\Phi$, including the condition
$\mathbf a=0$ corresponding to the empty subset of the basis of $F_{n+1}$.
A fixed finite system is solvable in a direct product
if and only if it is solvable in every coordinate.

Since $z$ is not a boundary, every $\varphi\in\Phi$ fails in $P$.
For each $\varphi$, choose a coordinate $i_\varphi$ where it fails,
and put $X=\{i_\varphi:\varphi\in\Phi\}$.
Then $|X|\le\rho$. Coordinate projection sends $z$ to a cycle
$z_X$ in $F_n\otimes_R\prod_{i\in X}M_i$.
Every system in $\Phi$ still fails at its selected coordinate.
Hence $z_X$ is not a boundary. This proves the assertion, and the
criterion for closure under direct products follows immediately.
For the assertion about Gorenstein flat modules, apply this result
in degree one and use \eqref{eq:detecting-test}, since direct products
over subsets of the index set are direct summands.
head: environment

label: rmk:boundary-systems
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:boundary-systems}
The finite systems in \eqref{eq:boundary-matrix} give a further criterion.
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. Choose $T$ as in
\eqref{eq:detecting-test}. For each finite subset of the basis in degree
one of a free resolution of $T$, let $\Phi$ be the associated systems
\eqref{eq:boundary-matrix}. The class $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under
direct products if and only if, for each such subset, one member of
$\Phi$ holds for every cycle supported on that subset over every
$G\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$.

If, for one such subset, no member of $\Phi$ holds for every cycle
supported on that subset over every $G\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$, choose for every
$\varphi\in\Phi$ a Gorenstein flat module and a tuple of coefficients
of a cycle for which $\varphi$ has no solution.
The chosen tuples determine a cycle in the direct product for which
every system in $\Phi$ has no solution. Hence the direct product of the chosen modules is not
Gorenstein flat.
Conversely, a single system valid on all coordinate cycles is
valid on the corresponding tuple in the direct product. Therefore every degree-one cycle
is a boundary, and \eqref{eq:detecting-test} applies.
head: environment

label: prop:finite-product-dimensions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:finite-product-dimensions}
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. If every direct product of at most $\rho$
Gorenstein flat $R$-modules has finite Gorenstein flat dimension,
then $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under arbitrary direct products.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, the finite dimensions have a uniform bound, as in
\cite[Proposition 2.4]{CI}. Otherwise,
for each $n<\omega$, choose such a direct product $P_n$ with
$\operatorname{Gfd}_RP_n>n$. After reindexing, $\prod_{n<\omega}P_n$ still has
at most $\rho$ Gorenstein flat factors. Its dimension is finite,
say $d$. Each $P_n$ is a direct summand, whence
$\operatorname{Gfd}_RP_n\le d$, a contradiction for $n>d$.

We now adapt the dimension-shifting argument in the proof of
\cite[Theorem 5.7]{CFH}. Let $d$ be the least uniform bound.
Suppose that $d>0$.
For an arbitrary family $(G_i)$ in $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ indexed by a set
of cardinality at most $\rho$, choose exact sequences
$0\to G_i\to F_i\to G_i'\to0$ from complete flat resolutions,
with $F_i$ flat and $G_i'$ Gorenstein flat.
Put $P=\prod_iG_i$ and $P'=\prod_iG_i'$.
Taking direct products gives $0\to P\to\prod_iF_i\to P'\to0$.
Since $R$ is right coherent, $\prod_iF_i$ is flat by
\cite[Theorem 2.1]{Chase}. We obtain
$\operatorname{Tor}_d^R(T,P)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{d+1}^R(T,P')=0$
by dimension shifting and Lemma~\ref{lem:detecting-dimensions}.
Thus $\operatorname{Gfd}_RP\le d-1$, contradicting minimality of $d$.
Consequently $d=0$, and
$\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under arbitrary direct products by
Theorem~\ref{thm:coordinate}.
head: environment

label: prop:detecting-syzygy
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:detecting-syzygy}
Let $R$ be a right coherent ring. For a family $(G_i)$ in $\mathcal{GF}(R)$, put
$P=\prod_iG_i$. Then
$\ker\tau_L=\ker(u\otimes_RP)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(T,P)$.
Consequently, $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under direct products if and only if
$L$ is $\mathcal{GF}(R)$-Mittag--Leffler.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $u\otimes_RG_i$ is injective for every $i$ by
\eqref{eq:detecting-test}. Since $F_T$ is free, $\tau_{F_T}$ is
injective. Naturality gives
$$
 \tau_{F_T}(u\otimes_RP)
 =\left(\prod_i(u\otimes_RG_i)\right)\tau_L.
$$
Since $\tau_{F_T}$ and $\prod_i(u\otimes_RG_i)$ are injective,
the two kernels agree.
The long exact Tor sequence of \eqref{eq:detecting-presentation}
identifies this kernel with $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(T,P)$.
For the relative Mittag--Leffler criterion for hereditary Tor-pairs,
see \cite[Theorem 2.1]{CI}.
head: environment

label: lem:stationary-intersection
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:stationary-intersection}
\label{prop:stationary-criterion}
For every $\lambda$, one has
$\bigcap_{\mu\ge\lambda}H_{j_{\mu\lambda}}(E_U)
=H_{j_\lambda}(E_U)=H_{u j_\lambda}(E_U)$.

The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The module $L$ is $\mathcal{GF}(R)$-Mittag--Leffler.
\item The module $L$ is $E_U$-stationary.
\item For every $\lambda$, there is $\mu\ge\lambda$ such that
$H_{j_{\mu\lambda}}(E_U)=H_{u j_\lambda}(E_U)$.
\end{enumerate}
Condition~(3) says that every map $L_\mu\to E_U$, restricted
to $L_\lambda$, extends to $F_T$. Here $\mu$ depends on $\lambda$,
but not on the map being extended.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h:L_\lambda\to E_U$ belong to each image in the intersection.
Introduce variables $x_a$ with values in $E_U$, one for every
$a\in L$. Require $x_{a+b}=x_a+x_b$ for all $a,b\in L$,
$x_{ar}=x_a r$ for all $a\in L$ and $r\in R$, and
$x_a=h(a)$ for all $a\in L_\lambda$. Every finite subsystem involves finitely many
elements of $L$. They lie in some finitely generated
$L_\mu\supseteq L_\lambda$, and an extension of $h$ to $L_\mu$
solves that subsystem. Since $E_U$ is pure-injective, algebraic
compactness supplies a solution of the entire system;
see \cite[Proposition 9.2]{Stenstrom}. It defines an extension $L\to E_U$.
This proves the first equality. Since $E_U\in T^\perp$,
\eqref{eq:detecting-presentation} implies that
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(F_T,E_U)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(L,E_U)$ is surjective. This proves the second
equality.

By the first assertion, the intersection of
the images is $H_{u j_\lambda}(E_U)$. The images stabilize if and
only if this intersection is attained at some stage. Thus the
conditions~(2) and~(3) are equivalent.

We use tensor--Hom adjunction. For a map $f:M\to N$
of $R^{\mathrm{op}}$-modules and an $R$-module $G$, the image of
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(f,G^+)$ is the annihilator of $\ker(f\otimes_RG)$ under
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R^{\mathrm{op}}}(M,G^+)\cong(M\otimes_RG)^+$.
Indeed, a character vanishing on the kernel defines a character
on the image and extends to $N\otimes_RG$, because
$\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is injective. Characters separate points
of quotient groups, so equality of these annihilators is equivalent
to equality of the kernels.

Assume condition~(1). Apply the criterion
\eqref{eq:relative-ML-stages} to $L$ with $Q=C_U$. The equal kernels give
$H_{j_{\mu\lambda}}(E_U)=H_{j_\lambda}(E_U)$, proving condition~(3).

Conversely, assume condition~(3). The extension property holds
with the same $\mu$ when $E_U$ is replaced by any direct product
of copies of $E_U$, since maps into a direct product are determined
by their coordinate maps. It also holds for every direct summand of such a direct product,
by projecting an extension to the summand. As shown above, every
$G^+$ with $G\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is a direct summand of a direct product of
copies of $E_U$. Hence the condition holds for every such $G^+$.
Since $G^+\in T^\perp$, one has
$H_{u j_\lambda}(G^+)=H_{j_\lambda}(G^+)$.
The annihilator observation gives
$\ker(j_\lambda\otimes_RG)=\ker(j_{\mu\lambda}\otimes_RG)$
for every such $G$. Thus \eqref{eq:relative-ML-stages} gives
condition~(1).
head: environment

label: rmk:pure-injectivity-stationarity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:pure-injectivity-stationarity}
In Proposition~\ref{lem:stationary-intersection}, pure-injectivity of
$E_U$ identifies the intersection of the restriction images with
$H_{j_\lambda}(E_U)$; the equality with $H_{u j_\lambda}(E_U)$ uses
$E_U\in T^\perp$. Closure of $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ under direct products requires the
restriction images $H_{j_{\mu\lambda}}(E_U)$ to stabilize at
$H_{u j_\lambda}(E_U)$. If $E_U$ is $\Sigma$-pure-injective,
then $L$ is $E_U$-stationary by \cite[Corollary 8.11(3)]{AHH},
and hence $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under direct products. Thus, for the ring
in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-counterexample}, $E_U$ is not
$\Sigma$-pure-injective.
head: environment

label: prop:canonical-bidual
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove $(4)\Rightarrow(1)$. Choose $d<\infty$ with
$\operatorname{Gfd}_RC_U^{++}\le d$. We first show that every direct product of
Gorenstein flat modules has Gorenstein flat dimension at most $d$.
Otherwise, there is a nonzero
$\operatorname{Tor}_{d+1}^R(T,\prod_{i\in X}G_i)$ with $|X|\le\rho$,
by Lemma~\ref{lem:detecting-dimensions} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:coordinate}.
Choose a free resolution of $T$ and a cycle representing a nonzero
class in its tensor product with $\prod_{i\in X}G_i$.
For each $i\in X$, choose a pure Gorenstein flat submodule
$H_i\subseteq G_i$ of cardinality at most $\rho$ containing the
finitely many coefficients in that coordinate, by
\cite[Lemma 2.25(a)]{GT} and Lemma~\ref{lem:character-Tor}.
Since the terms of the resolution are free, the inclusion
$\prod_{i\in X}H_i\subseteq\prod_{i\in X}G_i$ induces a
monomorphism in each degree. Hence the same expression defines a
cycle after tensoring the resolution with $\prod_{i\in X}H_i$.
It is not a boundary, since its image in the resolution tensored with
$\prod_{i\in X}G_i$ is not a boundary.

Since $|X|\le\rho$, $D=\bigoplus_{i\in X}H_i$ is isomorphic
to a direct summand of $C_U$.
The module $\prod_{i\in X}H_i$ embeds
purely into $D^{++}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:product-into-bidual},
and hence into $C_U^{++}$.
Thus $\operatorname{Gfd}_R(\prod_{i\in X}H_i)\le d$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:detecting-dimensions}, a contradiction.
This proves that finite Gorenstein flat dimension of $C_U^{++}$ bounds the
Gorenstein flat dimensions of all direct products of modules in $\mathcal{GF}(R)$.
These direct products are Gorenstein flat by
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-product-dimensions}.

For $(2)\Rightarrow(1)$, suppose that $C_U^\rho$ is Gorenstein flat.
If $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ were not closed under direct products, the coordinate
projection and the choice of pure submodules used for
$(4)\Rightarrow(1)$, applied in degree one, would give a direct product $\prod_{i\in X}H_i$ with
$|X|\le\rho$ and $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(T,\prod_{i\in X}H_i)\ne0$.
Each $H_i$ is isomorphic to a direct summand of $C_U$, so
$\prod_{i\in X}H_i$ is isomorphic to a direct summand of $C_U^X$,
and hence of $C_U^\rho$, a contradiction.

Assume condition~(1). Then $C_U^\rho\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$, proving
condition~(2).
Together with the already established closure under pure
submodules and direct limits, closure under direct products makes
$\mathcal{GF}(R)$ definable.
Definable classes are closed under character biduals
(see \cite[Corollary 4.6]{MP}). Hence condition~(3) holds, and it implies condition~(4).
Finally, $(C_U^{++})^+=E_U^{++}$, so
$(3)\Longleftrightarrow(5)$ and $(4)\Longleftrightarrow(6)$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:detecting-dimensions}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Conditions~(1) and~(2) are equivalent by
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-product-dimensions}. Their equivalence
with conditions~(3) and~(4) follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:detecting-syzygy} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:stationary-criterion}, and their equivalence
with conditions~(5) and~(6) follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-bidual}. Since $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed
under pure submodules and direct limits, we obtain condition~(7)
from the definition of a definable class (see \cite{Prest,SS}).
Conditions~(1) and~(8) are equivalent by
\cite[Corollary 3.5(c)]{RS}.
head: environment

label: cor:countable-intersections
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:countable-intersections}
The modules $N_n$ form a decreasing sequence with $N_n\prec F$
for every $n$. Its intersection $N=\bigcap_nN_n$ has infinite Gorenstein
flat dimension. Therefore $(\mathcal{GF}(R),\prec)$ has finite character
and L\"owenheim--Skolem number $\rho=|k|+\aleph_0$, but does not admit intersections.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $F/N_n\cong M/M_n\cong B^n$, closure under finite direct products and the
resolving property imply $N_n\prec F$. Moreover,
$N=\ker\pi$. For every $q\geq1$, the exact sequence
$0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0$
gives $\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(I,N)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_{q+1}^R(I,M)\ne0$.
Thus $\operatorname{Gfd}_RN=\infty$. Finite character and the upper bound $\rho$
for the L\"owenheim--Skolem number follow from
\cite[Theorem 2.11]{ST} and \cite[Theorem 10.28]{GT}, respectively.
For the lower bound, apply the L\"owenheim--Skolem property to
$\{1\}\subseteq R\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$. Every submodule of $R$ containing
$1$ equals $R$, so the L\"owenheim--Skolem number is at least
$|R|=\rho$.
head: environment

label: rmk:known-intersection-examples
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:known-intersection-examples}
An example of a class of roots of $\operatorname{Ext}$ which does not admit
intersections is given in \cite[Example 2.11]{BET}.
A class of projective modules that is closed under direct products but
whose associated abstract elementary class does not admit
intersections is given in \cite[Example 10.31]{GT}.
For the ring $R$ in \eqref{eq:main-ring}, failure of intersections in
$(\mathcal{GF}(R),\prec)$ is witnessed by a decreasing countable sequence of
strong submodules of a free module whose intersection has infinite
Gorenstein flat dimension, by Corollary~\ref{cor:countable-intersections}.
head: environment

label: prop:tail-equivalence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:tail-equivalence}
\label{prop:large-cofinality}
The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The class $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under arbitrary direct products.
\item For every limit ordinal $\lambda$, every family
$(G_\beta)_{\beta<\lambda}$ in $\mathcal{GF}(R)$, and every epimorphism
$\pi:F\to P$ from a free module, $L_\alpha\prec F$ for all
$\alpha<\lambda$ implies
$\bigcap_{\alpha<\lambda}L_\alpha\prec F$.
\item The implication in condition~(2) holds whenever
$\lambda$ is an infinite cardinal with $\lambda\leq\rho$.
\end{enumerate}

In the notation above, if $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)>\rho$ and
$L_\alpha\prec F$ for every $\alpha<\lambda$, then
$\bigcap_{\alpha<\lambda}L_\alpha\prec F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is closed under direct products, then $F/\ker\pi\cong P$
is Gorenstein flat. Thus $\ker\pi\prec F$, proving condition~(2).
Condition~(2) implies condition~(3).

For $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$, we adapt the argument in the proof of
$(1)\Rightarrow(2)$ in \cite[Lemma 2.8]{BET}.
Suppose that $\mathcal{GF}(R)$ is not closed under direct products.
There is a least cardinal
$\lambda\leq\rho$ such that a direct product of $\lambda$ Gorenstein flat
modules is not Gorenstein flat, by Theorem~\ref{thm:coordinate}. Since finite direct products are Gorenstein flat, $\lambda$
is infinite. Choose such a direct product and an epimorphism from a free module as above.
Minimality gives $F/L_\alpha\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$ for every $\alpha<\lambda$.
Then $L_\alpha\prec F$ by the resolving property.
Condition~(3) would give $\ker\pi\prec F$, and hence
$P\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$, a contradiction.

For the final assertion, assume that $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)>\rho$
and $L_\alpha\prec F$ for every $\alpha<\lambda$.
Each direct product $\prod_{\beta<\alpha}G_\beta$, with $\alpha<\lambda$,
belongs to $\mathcal{GF}(R)$. Every subset $X\subseteq\lambda$
of cardinality at most $\rho$ is bounded in $\lambda$. Thus
$\prod_{\beta\in X}G_\beta$ is a direct summand of one of these
direct products and is Gorenstein flat.
We have $P\in\mathcal{GF}(R)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:coordinate},
and hence $\ker\pi\prec F$.
head: environment

label: rmk:cofinality-restriction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:cofinality-restriction}
For the ring $R$ in \eqref{eq:main-ring}, condition~(2) of
Proposition~\ref{prop:tail-equivalence} fails at $\lambda=\omega$,
by Corollary~\ref{cor:countable-intersections}.
The implication in condition~(2) holds whenever
$\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)>\rho=|k|+\aleph_0$,
by the final assertion of Proposition~\ref{prop:large-cofinality}. Hence the cofinality restriction
cannot be omitted. If instead every $L_\alpha$ is pure in $F$, then
each direct product $\prod_{\beta<\alpha}G_\beta$, with $\alpha<\lambda$,
is flat and every $G_\beta$ is flat.
Thus $P$ is flat by Chase's theorem (see \cite{Chase}),
and $\ker\pi$ is pure in $F$.
The argument using Chase's theorem concerns the submodules
$L_\alpha=\pi^{-1}(P_\alpha)$ and does not assert closure under arbitrary
intersections of pure submodules.
head: environment
